answer: Use the sc-rx command, which shows the Receiving Secure Channel attributes: 'show sc-rx-<name>/<index> [sci-rx] [state] [association-number] [key-identifier] [next-packet-number]'. The 'state' attribute is the one that tells you usage: it is the state of the secure channel returned by the MKA stack, with values 'in-use' (Secure Association(s) under this Secure Channel is in use) and 'not-in-use' (no Secure Association(s) under this Secure Channel are in use). The AID is keyed by 'name', a String of length 0..64, plus 'index', the Receiving Secure Channel Index (uint8). 'sci-rx' is the Receiving Secure Channel Identifier, a hex-string of length 16. Access mode is Operational Mode and Candidate Configuration Mode; sc-rx is show-only.

sc-tx reports the Transmitting Secure Channel attributes and is show-only: there is no add, set or delete for it. Syntax is 'show sc-tx-<name>/<index> [sci-tx] [state] [association-number] [key-identifier] [next-packet-number]'. The key is 'name' (String, length 0..64) plus 'index', the Transmitting Secure Channel Index (uint8). 'sci-tx' is the Transmitting Secure Channel Identifier, a hex-string of length 16. 'state' is the state of the secure channel returned by the MKA stack, with values 'in-use' (Secure Association(s) under this Secure Channel is in use) and 'not-in-use' (no Secure Association(s) under this Secure Channel are in use). Access mode is Operational Mode and Candidate Configuration Mode.

A secure-application is an application that uses an X509v3 certificate as its digital identity. Assign its identity with 'set secure-application-<id> [active-certificate-id <value>] [verify-client-cert <value>]', where 'id' is a string of length 0..20 and 'active-certificate-id' is a string of length 0..128 holding the list of assigned certificates, for example 'set secure-application-WebGUI active-certificate-id client' or, for multiple, 'set secure-application-gRPC active-certificate-id certX,certY'. To require a certificate from clients, set 'verify-client-cert' to 'required' (client certificate is required and validated); the alternative is 'disabled' (client certificate is not requested), which is the default. For TLS Mutual Authentication this must be 'required'. Changes take effect for new TLS connections only and do not affect existing connections. 'show secure-application-<id>' also returns 'type' (server or client), 'in-use' (a leafref to ../active-certificate-id) and 'status' (enabled or disabled); 'show secure-applications' lists them all. Access mode is Operational and Candidate Configuration mode.

That is governed by 're-key-fail-policy' on the secure-entity, which indicates the NE's policy and consequent action when re-keying the IKE security association is unsuccessful. Values are 'kill-traffic' and 'continue-traffic', and the default is 'continue-traffic', so by default the node does not drop traffic. If you set 'kill-traffic', 'traffic-kill-offset' indicates the amount of time the system waits before killing all encrypted data security associations tied to that IKE SA; its range is 0..86400 seconds with a default of 0. Both are settable on add and set, for example 'add secure-entity-NE202-1-4-L1-1 supporting-facility optical-carrier-1-4-L1-1 remote-secure-entity '1-4-L1-1' re-key-fail-policy kill-traffic traffic-kill-offset 300'. The related 're-key-frequency' for the IKE SA with the far-end IKE peer ranges 3600..86400 seconds, default 28800.

No. secure-entity-sa-proposal is show-only: 'show secure-entity-sa-proposal-<name>/<number> [encryption-algorithm] [encryption-key-length] [integrity-algorithm] [dh-group]'. Every algorithm attribute has exactly one permitted value, which is also its default: 'encryption-algorithm' is aes-gcm-16, 'encryption-key-length' is key-length-256, 'integrity-algorithm' is none, and 'dh-group' (the Diffie-Hellman group advertised to the far-end secure entity peer) is ecp-521. The proposal 'number' likewise has the single value 1, default 1, and 'name' is the proposal name for the secure entity SA (string). Access mode is Operational Mode and Candidate Configuration Mode. So the secure entity SA algorithm set is fixed and only readable.

Through the security-policy-database object, whose key is the IKE peer itself: 'add security-policy-database-<ikev2-local-instance>/<ikev2-peer-name> [associated-secure-entity <value>]', with matching set, show and delete forms. 'ikev2-local-instance' is the name (ID) of the local IKE protocol daemon instance, 'ikev2-peer' is a reference to the IKE peer object (IKE SA), and 'associated-secure-entity' is the list of all SPD entries associated with this far-end peer for which IKE negotiates security associations (keys). All three are strings. Example on 1830 GX G40: 'add security-policy-database-ikev2-local-instance-1-6/ikev2-NE202-1-4 associated-secure-entity secure-entity-1-6-L1-1'. Access mode is Operational and Candidate Configuration mode.

Yes, using cdp, which manages manually configured CRL Distribution Points; each CDP supports download and auto-refreshing of a specified CRL. Use 'add cdp-<name> url <value> [enabled <value>] [refresh-interval <value>]', then set/show/delete, plus 'show cdps'. 'url' is the HTTP URL of the CRL in the form 'http://<host>[:<port>]/<path to crl file>', where host may be an IPv4/v6 address or DNS name and the path conventionally ends in .crl, for example http://crl.example.org/pki/myCA.crl. 'enabled' (true/false, default false) enables automatic download and periodic refresh; enabling immediately triggers a CRL auto-download, and when disabled no refresh or updates are performed but existing CRLs are unaffected. 'refresh-interval' takes either the special enum 'use-next-update' (next refresh time comes from the current CRL next-update field) or a '[xw] [xd] [xh] [xm] [xs]' string such as '2w', '5d 12h' or '1h 7m 30s'. Show also returns next-update-time, last-update-time and last-update-result (string 0..255). Requires System Administrator privilege; Operational and Candidate Configuration mode.

Use cert-gen, which generates a self-signed certificate, in Operational mode: 'cert-gen [-f] [certificate-name=]<value> [[days=]<value>] [[org-name=]<value>] [[common-name=]<value>] [[subject=]<value>] [SAN=]<value>] [auto-install <true|false>]'. Validity is set by 'days', the number of days a certificate is valid for, which defaults to 365. 'certificate-name' is a string of length 1..128, 'org-name' and 'common-name' are strings of length 1..64, and 'subject' (full certificate subject name) is a string of length 1..1024. You must specify either 'subject' or 'common-name' when generating the self-signed certificate. 'auto-install' (true/false, default true) auto-assigns the certificate to any secure-application without an active certificate. The '-f' flag forces the command without confirmation. Example: 'cert-gen -f certificate-name=self-signed-cert1 days=10 org-name=testorg common-name=testcert auto-install=true'.

Via cert-to-name, which defines a prioritized set of rules used to map an X.509 client certificate to a specific user identity; each rule either extracts a username from a certificate field or maps it directly, optionally restricted to a specific issuer in the trust chain. Use 'add cert-to-name-<id> map-type <value> field <value> mapped-user-name <value> criteria <value> [priority <value>] [issuer <value>] [enabled <value>] [label <value>]', plus set, show and delete. 'map-type' is 'extract' or 'map'. 'field' applies only when map-type is extract and selects the certificate attribute used to determine the identity: common-name, san-any, san-dns-name, san-ip-address, san-rfc822-name, san-upn or san-uri. 'mapped-user-name' is required only when map-type is 'map' and defines the local or remote user identity. 'criteria' defines the attributes and conditions required for the rule to be invoked. 'priority' ranges 1 to 255, 'issuer' filters to certificates from a specific issuer (value 'any'), and 'enabled' is True or False with default True. Example: 'add cert-to-name-rule_name map-type extract field san-dns-name'.

Use the certificate command in Operational mode. Delete with 'clear [-f] certificate [type=]<value> [id=]<value>', where 'type' is trusted, local or peer, and 'id' is the certificate ID (string, length 0..128) which must match a currently installed but unused certificate of that type; press <tab> to obtain the list of certificate-ids that can be cleared. Examples: 'clear certificate local certX', 'clear certificate type=trusted id=certY', 'clear certificate trusted id=root' (which prompts 'Are you sure? [y/n]'); '-f' forces without confirmation. The type field also accepts the bulk purge options purge-all-invalid, purge-all-unused, purge-all-expired, purge-local-unused and purge-peer-unused. To list what is installed, run 'show certificates', which displays all managed local/trusted/peer X509v3 certificates on the system that were imported by download mechanism in PKCS#12 or PKCS#7 secure bundles; 'show certificate-revocation' shows certificate revocations.

Use the crl clear command with a selective clear-target: 'clear [-f] crl [[clear-target=]<value>] [crl-name=]<value>'. The targets are 'single-crl' (remove the CRL specified in <crl-name>; this is the default and <crl-name> is mandatory and must match a currently installed CRL), 'purge-invalid-crls' (purge all invalid CRLs), 'purge-cached-crls' (purge all CRLs that were automatically cached from a configured CDP or certificate CDP extension) and 'purge-all-crls' (purge all CRLs). To drop only stale entries use 'clear crl purge-invalid-crls'; to remove one named list use 'clear crl single-crl myCA-1'. Use <tab> to obtain the list of CRL names that can be cleared. Check first with 'show crls' or 'show crl-<name>', where 'status' reports valid, expired or future and 'type' reports whether the CRL was installed 'manually' or 'cached' from a CDP. Clear runs in Operational mode; Candidate Configuration mode is only for the show command.

csr-gen generates a Certificate Signing Request from user provided information. The consequence of the command is the creation of a local-certificate in the 'pending-import' state, plus the output of a CSR in PKCS#10 PEM format. That CSR is then used with an external Certificate Authority to produce a full certificate, which is downloaded into the system to produce a complete local-certificate. So the node holds a half-formed local-certificate entry with the key pair until the signed certificate is imported. Syntax is 'csr-gen [certificate-name=]<value> ([[key-algorithm=]<value>] | [[key-from-certificate=]<value>]) [[signature-hash-algorithm=]<value>] [[metadata-template=]<value>] ... [[subject=]<value>] [[SAN=]<value>]'. Access mode is Operational mode. 'key-algorithm' defaults to eccp256; the subject's CN RDN is mandatory, for example 'csr-gen myCertificate subject='/CN=Nokia''.

Use display-cert with the 'display-type' parameter: 'display-cert [certificate=]<value> [display-type=]<value>'. The permitted values are 'all-certificate-hierarchy', 'certificate-details' and 'certificate-hierarchy', and the default is 'all-certificate-hierarchy'. So to see the trust chain rather than just the certificate's own fields, ask for a hierarchy display type; 'certificate-details' is the value that shows only the certificate's own details. 'certificate' is a string naming the certificate to display, and tab completion offers the installed names such as local-certificate-pace_client, local-certificate-server_cert, trusted-certificate-ca_root and trusted-certificate-pace_root. Access mode is Operational Mode and Candidate Configuration mode. The command shows the details of a certificate or a CSR.

Use the est command. Enrollment over Secure Transport enables automated certificate management over HTTPS, and the device's EST client replaces the complex, manual steps of the traditional CSR process. Syntax: 'est [target-command=]<value> [[est-ca=]<value>] [certificate-name=]<value> ([[key-algorithm=]<value>] | [[key-from-certificate=]<value>]) [[signature-hash-algorithm=]<value>] [[metadata-template=]<value>] ... [[http-user=]<value>] [[http-password=]<value>]'. 'target-command' selects the operation: 'cacerts', 'enroll' or 're-enroll'. 'est-ca' identifies the CA set for EST and defaults to 1. 'key-algorithm' accepts eccp256, eccp384, eccp251, rsa2048, rsa3072, rsa4096; 'signature-hash-algorithm' is sha512, sha384 or sha256 with default sha256; 'metadata-template' defaults to 'generic' with options from-existing-certificate, from-openssl-cnf, generic, generic-tls-server, generic-tls-client and generic-ikev2-identity. Example when a valid mTLS certificate does not exist: 'est enroll certificate-name=myNewCertificateA subject='/CN=NewCertA' http-user=<username> http-password=<password>'. Access mode is Operational and Candidate Configuration Mode.

Yes, through est-ca: 'set est-ca-<name> [explicit-ca-root <value>] [root-fingerprint <value>] [auto-re-enrollment <value>] [label <value>]'. 'auto-re-enrollment' specifies when re-enrollment is performed for all leaf certificates issued by this EST CA, expressed either as a number of days before expiration (1 to 365) or as a percentage of the 'not after date' minus 'not before date' interval, rounded up, accepted from 10% to 90% in increments of 10%; the value 'disabled' turns it off and is the default. If auto re-enrollment fails for any reason, the RE-ENROLL-FAIL alarm is raised for the affected certificate and re-enrollment is retried once per day until either it succeeds or the certificate becomes invalid, for example by expiring. The CA is pinned by 'explicit-ca-root', the trusted root certificate for the EST CA, together with 'root-fingerprint', which verifies the identity of the Root CA using a SHA-256 or SHA-512 hash to ensure a secure initial connection. Example: 'set est-ca-1 auto-re-enrollment 40'.

The EST server port is set by 'server-port' on the est-server object and defaults to 443. Yes, you can define more than one: est-server entries are keyed as '<name>/<server-name>', so 'add est-server-<name>/<server-name> server-address <value> [server-port <value>] [priority <value>] [enabled <value>] [path-segment <value>]' can be repeated, with matching set, delete and show forms. 'priority' defines the server's precedence and ranges from 1 to 10; if omitted, the priority defaults to the current lowest precedence (highest existing number) plus one, and if a priority of 10 already exists the value must be configured manually. 'enabled' is True or False with default True, and 'path-segment' is an optional label added to the EST base url (string, length 0..64). Example: 'add est-server-1/my-est-server server-address 10.23.55.123 server-port 8443'. Access mode is Operational and Candidate Configuration Mode.

Use import-certificate, which imports one or more certificates in PEM format into the NE: 'import-certificate {-i, <certificate type>} [<certificate-name>] <string in PEM format> [<passphrase>]'; 'import-certificate -h' displays help. The certificate type is local-certificate, trusted-certificate or peer-certificate. 'certificate-name' is the name by which the certificate will be known in the system, and 'passphrase' decodes encrypted input certificates (applies to trusted-certificate, local-certificate and bundles). The '-i' flag imports any intermediate certificates present in a PEM string bundle; for files with a single certificate it imports any intermediate certificates specified through the AIA extension. Root certificates need to be installed individually. If no certificate-name is given, the name is derived from the topmost certificate issuer /CN plus a numeric suffix, for example trusted-certificate-Nokia-1 and trusted-certificate-Nokia-2 for issuer /CN=Nokia. Examples: 'import-certificate local-certificate certificate-name=local-cert-1 <string in PEM format> <passphrase>' and 'import-certificate trusted-certificate certificate-name=bundle-1 -i <string in PEM format>'. Access mode is Operational mode.

Check the ISK object before clearing it: 'show ISK-<name> [CPU] [key-name] [key-serial-number] [issuer-name] [key-length] [key-payload] [is-key-in-use] [is-key-verified] [being-deleted] [KRK-name] [signature-hash-scheme] [signature-algorithm] [signature-payload] [signature-gen-time]', or 'show ISKs' for the list. 'is-key-in-use' indicates if the key is in use in this FRU (true/false, default false), 'is-key-verified' indicates if the key is verified in this FRU (true/false, default false), and 'being-deleted' is set to true once the system gets an ISK delete command, indicating the system is in the process of deletion and will soon delete this ISK. 'KRK-name' names the Image Root Key that signed this ISK. To remove one, use 'clear [-f] isk [key-name=]<value>', supplying the name of the key to be deleted (String, length 0..64), for example 'clear isk key-name=name'; '-f' forces the command without confirmation. Clear runs in Operational Mode; Candidate Configuration Mode is only for the show command.

Use the KRK commands, which show the list of Image Root Keys and KRK information: 'show KRKs' returns the list, and 'show KRK-<name> [CPU] [key-name] [key-serial-number] [issuer-name] [key-length] [key-payload]' returns one key's details, for example 'show KRK-1-5-0-KRK_E1'. 'name' is the unique representation of the object, 'CPU' is the identifier for member CPUs on cards and starts at 0 (uint8), 'key-name' is a String of length 0..64, 'key-serial-number' is a String, 'issuer-name' is the name of the CSA (Code Signing Appliance), a String of length 0..20, 'key-length' is the key length in bits (uint16), and 'key-payload' is the key payload in hex format, a String of length 0..1100. KRK is show-only; access mode is Operational Mode and Candidate Configuration Mode.

The key-replacement-package command: 'show key-replacement-package [KRP-name] [KRP-version] [key-name] [key-serial-number] [issuer-name] [key-length] [key-payload] [KRK-name] [signature-hash-scheme] [signature-algorithm] [signature-payload] [signature-gen-time] [install-status]'. It is show-only. 'KRP-version' is the package version, 'issuer-name' is the name of the CSA (Code Signing Appliance), a string of length 0..20, and 'KRK-name' is the name of the KRK (Image root key) that signed this ISK. 'signature-hash-scheme' is SHA2 256, SHA2 384 or SHA2 512; 'signature-algorithm' is ECDSA, RSA or none; 'signature-payload' is a hex string 0..1024; 'signature-gen-time' is a date-time in the format YYYY-MM-DDThh:mm:ssZ. 'install-status' indicates if this KRP has been installed in the system, with values not-installed, installing, installed and failed. Access mode is Operational mode and Candidate Configuration mode.

Yes, using the 'revocation-mode' attribute of local-certificate, which controls how the revocation status of the certificate is determined: 'set local-certificate-<id> [revocation-mode <value>] [alarm-report-control <value>] [label <value>]'. Values are 'auto', 'force-revoked' and 'force-unrevoked', with 'auto' as the default. Setting 'force-revoked' forces the node to treat the certificate as revoked; 'force-unrevoked' forces the opposite. 'id' is a String of length 1..128 matching the pattern for certificate names. 'show local-certificate-<id>' also returns 'status' (valid, revoked, expired, untrusted, future, pending-import for a CSR awaiting import, plus the legacy in-use, unused and available values) and 'used-by', the list of foreign keys representing secure-applications, ikev2-peers and so on presently using the certificate. 'alarm-report-control' is allowed or inhibited, default allowed. Access mode is Operational Mode and Candidate Configuration Mode.

Use 'add ocsp-server-<name> url <value> priority <value> [enabled <value>]', with 'set ocsp-server-<name> [priority <value>] [enabled <value>]', 'delete ocsp-server-<name>' and 'show ocsp-server-<name> [url] [enabled] [priority] [last-query]'. Order is set by 'priority', a uint8 in the range 1..10, used to sort the OCSP responders in order of precedence: lower numbered OCSP responders are consulted before higher numbered ones, so give the responder you want tried first the lowest number. 'url' is the HTTP URL of the OCSP responder in the form 'http://<host>[:<port>]', where host may be an IPv4/v6 address or DNS name and the port is optional (otherwise the default HTTP port 80 is used); it is a string of length 0..1024 matching pattern 'http://([^\s/$.?#][^\s/]*)'. 'enabled' (true/false, default false) controls whether this server is consulted for revocation status, and 'last-query' is the timestamp of the last successful query ('never' or a date-and-time). Example: 'add ocsp-server-1 url http://1.2.3.4:8101 priority 3 enabled true'.

A peer-certificate is the X509v3 end-entity certificate that represents a trusted 'remote peer' certificate for the L1 encryption secure application. Manage it with 'set peer-certificate[-id] [alarm-report-control <value>] [label <value>] [revocation-mode <value>]' and 'show peer-certificate[-id] ... [white-listed] ...'. The 'white-listed' flag (true/false, default false) means that if true, the peer-certificate does not have an associated trust-chain and was explicitly white-listed at import time; otherwise it has an associated trust-chain. 'trust-chain' is a leafref to /ne/system/security/certificates/trusted-certificate/id. 'status' values are revoked, expired, pending-import, untrusted, future, valid and unsupported (with in-use, unused, available and invalid deprecated in favour of valid/untrusted plus the used-by attribute). 'revocation-mode' is auto, force-revoked or force-unrevoked, default auto; 'alarm-report-control' is inhibited or allowed, default allowed. Access mode is Operational Mode and Candidate Configuration Mode.

SSH is configured with 'set ssh [enabled <value>] [port <value>] [pre-login-message <value>] [post-login-message <value>]' and read with 'show ssh'. The 'port' attribute is the port listening for ssh login that goes directly to shell; its range is 1..65535 and its default is 8022. It is not on by default: 'enabled', which enables direct access to shell via ssh, takes true or false and defaults to false. 'pre-login-message' is the welcome message displayed before user login (String, length 0..1440) with no default, and 'post-login-message' is displayed after login (String, length 0..1440) and defaults to the standard warning banner stating the system is restricted to authorized users for business purposes and may be monitored. The ssh object is managed by the system and cannot be manually deleted. Access mode is Operational mode and Candidate Configuration mode.

Add an ssh-authorized-key for that user. Each authorized key entry contains a trusted public key for SSHv2 user authentication. Use 'add ssh-authorized-key-<user-name>/<key-id> public-key <value> [label <value>]', with 'set ssh-authorized-key-<user-name>/<key-id> [label <value>]', 'show ssh-authorized-key-<user-name>/<key-id> [public-key-algorithm] [public-key] [label]' and 'delete ssh-authorized-key-<user-name>/<key-id>'. 'user-name' is the user owning the authorized key and can be a local or remote user (String, 0...32); 'key-id' is a unique identifier (name) for this entry (String, 1...64). 'public-key' is the SSHv2 (OpenSSH Portable) host public key component encoded in PEM format as '<key type><SPACE>...base64 encoded OpenSSH public key...<SPACE><comment>', a String of 0..2048 characters. 'public-key-algorithm' is read back as ecdsa-sha2-nistp256, ecdsa-sha2-nistp384, ecdsa-sha2-nistp521, ssh-rsa2048, ssh-rsa3072 or ssh-rsa4096. Example: 'add ssh-authorized-key-admin/1 public-key AAAAE2VjZHNh...'. Deleting prompts for confirmation. Access mode is Operational mode and Candidate Configuration mode.
